inherent_safety_characteristic: Graphite moderation allows positive void coefficient; no containment building; channel-type design allows on-line refueling; unique design with known instability at low power
Chernobyl_RBMK_relevance: RBMK is the reactor type that exploded; see reactor_physics_REAL.csv; rbmk_void_coefficient_physics_REAL.csv; rbmk_safety_modifications_REAL.csv

inherent_safety_characteristic: Negative void coefficient = self-limiting; loss of coolant reduces moderation → power drops automatically; pressurized coolant remains liquid (no boiling at operating pressure)
Chernobyl_RBMK_relevance: Fundamental physics contrast to RBMK; negative void coefficient prevents runaway void feedback; used as reference design for comparing RBMK deficiencies in INSAG-7

inherent_safety_characteristic: Similar to PWR but boiling in core; steam voids affect neutron economy; still inherently safer than RBMK because water is primary moderator; void coefficient less negative than PWR; Fukushima-Daiichi used BWR Mark-1 design
Chernobyl_RBMK_relevance: BWR had better inherent safety than RBMK; Fukushima-Daiichi was BWR; containment systems worked during SCRAM but hydrogen explosions occurred in turbine buildings; compare to Chernobyl where no containment existed

inherent_safety_characteristic: Soviet-designed PWR; negative void coefficient unlike RBMK; Western reactor physics fundamentals; VVER was running simultaneously with RBMK in USSR 1986; considered safer than RBMK by most analysts
Chernobyl_RBMK_relevance: USSR had both RBMK (Chernobyl; Leningrad; Kursk; Smolensk) and VVER (Novovoronezh; Balakovo; Kalinin) running in 1986; VVER physics inherently safer; post-Chernobyl: Soviet reactor program shifted toward VVER for new construction
source: WNA VVER profile; IAEA PRIS; INSAG-7

inherent_safety_characteristic: Heavy water provides efficient neutron economy; on-line refueling with natural uranium (no enrichment needed); positive void coefficient similar to RBMK physics but smaller magnitude; TWO independent SCRAM systems (unlike RBMK single)
Chernobyl_RBMK_relevance: CANDU shares the positive void coefficient characteristic with RBMK but has better designed defense in depth (two independent SCRAM systems; containment); used in comparison to RBMK in INSAG-7 analysis; CANDU has not had a major accident
source: INSAG-7 Section 4.4; WNA CANDU; AECL design documents

inherent_safety_characteristic: Metallic fuel has very strong Doppler feedback; passive reactivity shutdown from thermal expansion; inherently walk-away safe designs; higher neutron energy = no xenon poisoning; burns actinides (reduces waste radioactivity)
Chernobyl_RBMK_relevance: Gen IV designs address RBMK's fundamental instabilities; no xenon pit; passive safety; relevant context for what changed in reactor design post-Chernobyl
source: IAEA Gen IV INPRO; World Nuclear Association Gen IV; USAEC Gen IV roadmap

inherent_safety_characteristic: Liquid fuel drains passively to subcritical geometry on power loss (freeze plug); no fuel melt possible (fuel already liquid); inherently safe; graphite moderator (if used) but fuel dissolved in coolant = different void physics than RBMK
Chernobyl_RBMK_relevance: Post-Chernobyl design concept; addresses fuel melt scenario by design; freeze plug concept means loss of power = automatic shutdown and drain; relevant as contrast to RBMK design failures
source: Haubenreich 1970; Engel 1980 ORNL; Terrestrial Energy; Moltex Safety Case

inherent_safety_characteristic: Modified RBMK is safer: void coefficient 4-10x smaller; graphite tips removed from control rods; ORM minimum 30 rods; ORM monitoring automated; SCRAM time reduced 18→12s; enrichment 2.0→2.8%; operating procedures strengthened
Chernobyl_RBMK_relevance: 11 modified RBMK units continue operating in Russia 2026 (40 years after Chernobyl); WNA and IAEA consider modified RBMK safe at operating power; they have not had accidents since 1986 modifications
source: rbmk_safety_modifications_REAL.csv; WNA RBMK 2024; IAEA operational safety reviews
